query: In NIST DTSA-II, creating a quantification standard from a measured EDS spectrum requires adequate counting statistics. Why would a spectrum extracted or summed from an EDS spectrum-image (X-ray map) of an AlSi10Mg alloy fail signal-to-noise or precision checks even for major elements like Al and Si? What total counts or dose are recommended for standard spectra, and is the recommended practice to acquire several long point/raster spectra (e.g. four 60-second acquisitions), check for outliers, and sum them?

info.name: read_text
info.description:
Given a list of text names, read their contents.

This tool is valuable to read the full contents of specific parts of documents,
complementing the `gather_evidence` tool's indirect approach.
This can be an especially useful tool if `gather_evidence` does not find evidence,
but you think it is very likely that specific documents are still relevant to the question.

text_name_list.description:
A list of up to 10 text names to read.
These text names can be any valid text names retrieved by other tools.
text_name_list.title: Text Name List

info.name: view_images
info.description:
Retrieve images from a document.

Use this tool when you need to see figures, tables, or other visual content.
The tool works by asking a weaker LLM agent to scan through the document, looking for
visual content matching the query you provide. When the agent finds matches, it will
crop the page to the relevant region. It can be tasked to return multiple images,
if desired. Note that the weaker LLM may be worse at *understanding* images than
you, so double-check its conclusions about the returned images. It is also stateless,
i.e. it will not remember what you have asked it to find in the past.

Use this tool carefully. It is difficult to retrieve images, and the images
themselves will fill up your context window quickly. Here are some guidelines:
1. ALWAYS use this tool if the question explicitly mentions 'Table X' or 'Figure Y'.
   These questions require visual content and cannot be answered with text alone.
2. Use this tool as a fallback when gather_evidence fails repeatedly (2+ times
   returning 'No relevant evidence'). This suggests the answer may be in visual content.
3. When gather_evidence returns text mentioning 'see Figure X' or 'shown in Table Y',
   you should call this tool to examine that specific visual reference.
4. Only call this tool after directly inspecting relevant text with read_text
   to confirm the document likely contains the visual you need.
5. Don't use this tool in a broad-spectrum way (don't call on many documents
   just to see what might be relevant).
6. Never call this tool in parallel with itself.
7. Users like visual evidence, so call this tool at least once before answering so you
   can provide some image citations in the answer. Add this to your plan so you do not forget.
   For images to be presented to the user, they must be cited in the final answer after retrieval
   by this tool. You may ignore this instruction if the request is for the question is asking
   for a specific piece of information and is not an open-ended research question.
8. NEVER cite full-page images in your final answer, unless they are full-page panels figures or
   tables. Cite relevant cropped regions if available, otherwise consider calling this tool again
   to find a smaller region that answers the query.

query.description:
Query to search for visual content in the document. If you know the specific
figure/table/formula you are looking for, you can specify it here (e.g. "find me
Figure 3" or "extract the table on page 10"). You can also request based on content
(e.g. "find me all volcano plots of gene X" or "I need the formula for the growth rate").
You can even include explicit instructions for the LLM agent to follow (if helpful, not
necessarily required). The more specific and clear your query is here, the higher the
chance of success.
query.title: Query

text_name.description: Name of a text chunk (e.g., 'smith2023example pages 1-5').
text_name.title: Text Name

info.name: create_artifact
info.description:
Create an artifact that can be used in the final answer, based on information
you have collected so far.

How it works: the full message history thus far is passed to another LLM,
along with the question and your description. The LLM is tasked to create
an artifact that matches your specifications, including a title, caption,
and markdown content. You drive the process by specifying the type and
describing what you want.

Only use this tool *after* you have gathered sufficient evidence or
information to create a new artifact. Do not call this tool in parallel
with tools that are searching for information or evidence that would be
necessary to create this artifact.

It is very helpful after calls to several search tools,
after calls to the `gather_evidence` tool, but it is not required.
However, it should be called before the `answer` tool at
least one time, but more may be given if specifically helpful for
the task, so that the `answer` tool can use the artifacts for the answer.

An artifact can be any string representable fact or list of facts,
formatted using markdown syntax. The artifact will be generated as one of
the following types:
- table: Markdown tables with rows and columns (e.g., findings, methods, molecules)
- code_block: Code snippets in fenced code blocks
- blockquote: Quoted text or important facts (using > prefix)
- image: AI-generated image (chart, diagram, or visualization)

Each artifact consists of:
- A short title (3-8 words) that names what the artifact contains
- A caption (1-2 sentences) describing what the artifact shows and why it's useful
- Markdown content in a single element type (validated automatically with retries if needed)
  For image type, content is a markdown image embed ``![title](data:image/png;base64,...)``,
  embedding the PNG directly as a base64 data URL.

artifact_type.description:
Artifact type to create. Must be one of: table,
code_block, blockquote, image.
artifact_type.title: Artifact Type

description.description:
Description of what you want in the artifact. Be specific
about what information should be included, how it should be organized,
and what columns/sections/content you want. This guides the summary LLM.
For image type, describe the visual you want generated in detail.
description.title: Description

info.name: patent_search
info.description:
Search for patents to increase the patent count.

Repeat previous calls with the same query to continue a search.
Only repeat a maximum of three times.
This tool can be called concurrently.
This tool introduces novel patents, so invoke it when just beginning
or when unsatisfied with the current evidence.

query.description:
A search query for patents (using Google Patents). Never include temporal
filters here (e.g. specific years or dates); instead use the `after` and `before`
arguments. Never include author filters here; instead use the `inventor` argument.
Supports the following syntax, but they can be brittle and are not preferred; try
simple queries where possible:
- Boolean operators: AND (default), OR, and - (NOT)
- Exact phrases: "quoted text"
- Proximity: NEAR/x, ADJ/x (ordered), WITH (20 words), SAME (200 words)
- Field search: TI=(title), AB=(abstract), CL=(claims)
- CPC codes: cpc:A01B or CPC=B60R22/low (includes children)
- Wildcards: ? (0-1 char), * (0+ chars), # (exactly 1 char)
- Chemistry: exact molecule names, SSS=molecule (substructure),
  ~molecule (similar), SMILES strings, SMARTS=pattern, InChI keys,
  CL=~molecule (chemistry in claims)
query.title: Query

after.description:
Minimum patent date. Format: YYYYMMDD.
Example: '20150101' for patents after Jan 1, 2015.

Example: '20200101' for patents before Jan 1, 2020.
before.title: Before

date_type.description:

info.name: clinical_trials_search
info.description:
Search for clinical trials, with support for repeated calls and concurrent execution.

Will add new clinical trials to the state, and return metadata about the number of trials found.

query.description:
The search query string. Supports complex boolean expressions, field-specific
searches, and query modifiers through operators. All configuration is done through
operators in the query string.
Query Syntax:
    Basic Search:
        Simple text automatically uses default EXPANSION[Relaxation] and COVERAGE[Contains]
        >>> "heart attack"

    Modified Search:
        Use operators to modify search behavior:
        >>> 'EXPANSION[None]COVERAGE[FullMatch]"exact phrase"'
        >>> 'EXPANSION[Concept]heart attack'

    Field Search:
        Specify fields using AREA operator:
        >>> 'AREA[InterventionName]aspirin'
        >>> 'AREA[Phase]PHASE3'

    Location Search:
        Use SEARCH operator for compound location queries:
        >>> 'cancer AND SEARCH[Location](AREA[LocationCity]Boston AND AREA[LocationState]Massachusetts)'

    Complex Boolean:
        Combine terms with AND, OR, NOT and parentheses:
        >>> '(cancer OR tumor) AND NOT (EXPANSION[None]pediatric OR AREA[StdAge]CHILD)'

    Date Ranges:
        Use RANGE to specify date ranges with formats like "yyyy-MM" or "yyyy-MM-dd".
        Note that MIN and MAX can be used for open-ended ranges:
        >>> AREA[ResultsFirstPostDate]RANGE[2015-01-01, MAX]

Operators:
    EXPANSION[type]: Controls term expansion
        - None: Exact match only, case and accent sensitive
        - Term: Includes lexical variants (plurals, spellings)
        - Concept: Includes UMLS synonyms
        - Relaxation: Relaxes adjacency requirements (default)
        - Lossy: Allows missing partial terms

    COVERAGE[type]: Controls text matching
        - FullMatch: Must match entire field
        - StartsWith: Must match beginning of field
        - EndsWith: Must match end of field
        - Contains: Must match part of field (default)

    AREA[field]: Specifies field to search
        - See Field Reference for available fields

    SEARCH[type]: Groups field searches
        - Location: Groups location-related fields
        - Study: Groups study-related fields

Usage Notes:
    - All search expressions are implicitly OR expressions
    - Operator precedence (highest to lowest): terms/source operators, NOT/context operators, AND, OR
    - Use quotes for exact phrase matching: "heart attack"
    - Use parentheses for grouping: (heart OR cardiac) AND attack
    - Use backslash to escape operators: \AND
    - Default expansion is EXPANSION[Relaxation]
    - Default coverage is COVERAGE[Contains]

Field Reference:
    High Priority Fields (weight >= 0.8):
        - NCTId (1.0): Trial identifier
        - Acronym (1.0): Study acronym
        - BriefTitle (0.89): Short title
        - OfficialTitle (0.85): Full official title
        - Condition (0.81): Medical condition
        - InterventionName (0.8): Primary intervention name
        - OverallStatus: Trial status

    Medium Priority Fields (0.5-0.79):
        - InterventionOtherName (0.75): Alternative intervention names
        - Phase (0.65): Trial phase
        - StdAge (0.65): Standard age groups
        - Keyword (0.6): Study keywords
        - BriefSummary (0.6): Short description
        - SecondaryOutcomeMeasure (0.5): Secondary outcomes

    Low Priority Fields (< 0.5):
        - DesignPrimaryPurpose (0.3): Primary purpose of study
        - StudyType (0.3)
        - Various descriptive, location, and administrative fields

Supported Enums:
    Phase:
        - EARLY_PHASE1: Early Phase 1
        - PHASE1: Phase 1
        - PHASE2: Phase 2
        - PHASE3: Phase 3
        - PHASE4: Phase 4
        - NA: Not Applicable

    StandardAge:
        - CHILD: Child
        - ADULT: Adult
        - OLDER_ADULT: Older Adult

    Status:
        - RECRUITING: Currently recruiting participants
        - ACTIVE_NOT_RECRUITING: Active but not recruiting
        - COMPLETED: Study completed
        - ENROLLING_BY_INVITATION: Enrolling by invitation only
        - NOT_YET_RECRUITING: Not yet recruiting
        - SUSPENDED: Study suspended
        - TERMINATED: Study terminated
        - WITHDRAWN: Study withdrawn
        - AVAILABLE: Available

        - TEMPORARILY_NOT_AVAILABLE: Temporarily not available
        - APPROVED_FOR_MARKETING: Approved for marketing
        - WITHHELD: Withheld
        - UNKNOWN: Unknown status

    StudyType:
        - INTERVENTIONAL: Interventional studies
        - OBSERVATIONAL: Observational studies
        - EXPANDED_ACCESS: Expanded access studies

    PrimaryPurpose:
        - TREATMENT: Treatment
        - PREVENTION: Prevention
        - DIAGNOSTIC: Diagnostic
        - ECT: Educational/Counseling/Training
        - SUPPORTIVE_CARE: Supportive Care
        - SCREENING: Screening
        - HEALTH_SERVICES_RESEARCH: Health Services Research

info.name: gather_evidence
info.description:
Given a specific question, gather evidence from full-text of documents that have been retrieved by
previous tool calls.

Here is how the tool works: the provided question is posed to all texts retrieved thus far
by other tools. An LLM sees each text independently and is prompted to find information relevant
to the question.

That is, we sample evidence `e \sim LLM(prompt, text, q)` for each text. We only return pieces of
evidence `e` that are sufficiently relevant to the question; if the text is irrelevant, then `e`
is not included in the final response of this tool. Note that this LLM does not see the conversation
history thus far, only the question and each text. Note that it only sees text, no images or other
media from the contents (though tables and formulae may be parseable in some cases).

Think of this tool as an efficient way to deeply scan all retrieved documents for evidence. It
is complementary to the `read_text` tool, which can be used to directly inspect a subset of the
retrieved documents.

A valuable time to invoke this tool is after another tool finds potentially relevant documents.
Feel free to invoke this tool in parallel with other tools, but do not call this tool in parallel with itself.
Only invoke this tool when the document count is above zero, or this tool will be useless.

If you call this tool 2+ times and repeatedly get 'No relevant evidence found',
consider whether the answer might be in visual content (figures/tables) rather than text,
and use appropriate tools if available to access that content.

Once you receive evidence from this tool:

1. Read Carefully: Don't skim. The evidence may contain multiple similar terms
   or values—make sure you identify the RIGHT one.

2. For Comparative Questions: If the question asks "which X has greatest Y",
   check that the evidence includes information about ALL relevant X options, not
   just one or two. If you only see partial information, gather more evidence.

3. Check for Noise: Verify that numbers or terms aren't just metadata
   (page numbers, reference IDs, dates). Look for the value in meaningful
   scientific context.

4. Context Matters: A term appearing 71 times doesn't mean it's always the answer.
   Verify which occurrence actually answers the question asked.

If the evidence doesn't clearly answer the question, gather more evidence before
concluding. Don't guess based on partial information.

question.description: Specific question to gather evidence for.
question.title: Question

text_name_focus_list.description:
if there are known text names that are relevant to the question,
you can specify them here. This will ensure that the tool will look at these text names
first, and then look at the rest of the evidence. If left as `None`, an embedding
search will be performed on underlying content to find most relevant texts.
text_name_focus_list.title: Text Name Focus List

info.name: update_plan
info.description:
Update the plan for a specific or new objective using a JSON string to create or
replace the existing objective.

The updated_json should be a JSON string representing a single plan objective object.

You may use this tool to update an objective, create a new one, or change
strategy if the current plan is not working. Only change strategy significantly
as a last resort, after trying very hard to make the current plan work.

Only mark an objective as completed if you are absolutely sure that it has been fully
met. If it is only partially met, you may add additional objectives to the plan for
what is missing.

plan_objective_id.description: The id of the objective to update.
plan_objective_id.title: Plan Objective Id

updated_plan_objective_json.description:
A JSON string representing the updated objective.
It should be a dictionary with the with the following keys:
- "id": (int) an integer id matching plan_objective_id, if not found, a new objective is created.
- "objective": (str) a human readable description of the objective's goal
- "rationale": (str) a human readable rationale
    describing why this objective is necessary and appropriate for the query.
- "status": (str) updated task status, default to pending,
    one of: pending, in-progress, or completed.
    "pending" is yet to be started,
    "in-progress" is the current objective being solved,
    "completed" is successfully completed with acceptance criteria met.
- "result": (str|None) The result of the objective, default to None.
- "evaluation": (str|None) Description of why the objective result
    meets the criteria for being complete. Default to None.
updated_plan_objective_json.title: Updated Plan Objective Json

info.name: collect_cited_papers_in_evidence
info.description:
Collect papers by traversing the citations of relevant papers to increase the paper count.

This tool has no effect if called when paper count or relevant papers are zero.
This tool will find papers that are likely to lead to more relevant evidence.
The papers found have a higher chance of relevance because this tool starts from relevant evidence.
This tool's usefulness increases with the amount of gathered evidence as there's more citations to consider.

info.name: create_plan
info.description:
Create a plan for to construct a thorough and accurate answer.

Decompose the input task into a set of sub-objectives that need to
be met in order to form the answer. Subsequently, when working on solving
the query, you can focus on these objectives one by one. Note that the
`update_plan` tool allows you to change the objectives if needed.

In addition to the objectives you deem necessary, add one final objective
to call the `answer` tool with your final answer, so that you do not
forget to submit your answer.

plan_json.description:
A JSON string representing the plan. It should be a dictionary
with top-level key "objectives", whose value is a list of objectives.
Each objective should be a dictionary with the following keys:
- "id": (int) an integer id for the plan objective
- "objective": (str) a human readable description of the objective's goal
- "rationale": (str) a human readable rationale
    describing why this objective is necessary and appropriate for the query.
- "status": (str) updated task status, default to pending,
    one of: pending, in-progress, or completed.
    "pending" is yet to be started,
    "in-progress" is the current objective being solved,
    "completed" is successfully completed with acceptance criteria met.
- "result": (str|None) The result of the objective, default to None.
- "evaluation": (str|None) Description of why the objective result
    meets the criteria for being complete. Default to None.
plan_json.title: Plan Json

info.name: answer
info.description:
Submit your final answer to the user. You MUST call this tool on your final answer.
If you mark all objectives as completed but have not yet called this tool, then
the answer will not be submitted. Note that this tool should only be called once, as it
immediately terminates the run and submits the answer.

Write an answer based on the evidence from gather_evidence results in message history.
If the context provides insufficient information, provide a partial answer and explain
why it is partial (e.g. the question is currently an open question in the field,
you were unable to obtain certain papers, etc.).

For each part of your answer, indicate which sources most support it via citation IDs at
the end of sentences, like (pqac-0000ABCD).
You are only allowed to cite available context IDs, indicated in previous messages by "Context IDs that may be cited:".
## Valid citation examples, only use comma/space delimited parentheticals:

- (pqac-0000ABCD, pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000IJKL)

## Invalid citation examples:

- (pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD;pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD-pqac-0000EFGH)
- pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH
- Example's work pqac-0000ABCD
- (pages pqac-0000ABCD)
- ![description](pqac-0000ABCD)
- ()

Do not concatenate citation ids, just use them as-is.

When writing your answer, embed artifacts if relevant artifacts have been previously
created by the `create_artifact` tool. To embed an artifact, simply include this in your
answer, on its own line and without any additional formatting (i.e. no backticks, code fences,
quotes, additional tags, etc.).
Always provide at least some introductory sentence or paragraph before referring to an artifact,
so that the artifact is properly contextualized.
Here is an example reference to an artifact with ID "artifact-XY":
<artifact id="artifact-XY"/>

Valid artifact IDs are indicated in previous messages by 'Artifact IDs that may be injected into the answer:'.


Double-check your answer:

1. Evidence Match: Re-read the specific evidence snippets you're citing. Does your
   answer actually match what they say? Don't rely on memory from 20+ messages ago.

2. For Comparative Questions ("which X has greatest/maximum/highest Y"):
   - Did you examine ALL options mentioned in the evidence?
   - Did you explicitly compare their values?
   - Example: If evidence mentions "Pancreatic: 0.92, Liver: 0.85, Lung: 0.78",
     verify you compared all three, not just two.

3. For Specific Value Questions ("How many", "What is the", specific terms):
   - Does the exact value you're stating appear in the evidence?
   - Are you extracting from the right context (not noise like page numbers)?

4. Sanity Check: Read your answer. Does it directly address what was asked?

Don't use Markdown image syntax like ![...](...) to reference media in your answer,
because media get automatically linked by the system based on your answer's citations.

Write in the style of a scientific article, with concise sentences and
coherent paragraphs. This answer will be used directly,
so do not add any extraneous information.

answer.description: valid answer, cited with citation IDs.
answer.title: Answer

messages.content:
Use the tools to answer the question: In NIST DTSA-II, creating a quantification standard from a measured EDS spectrum requires adequate counting statistics. Why would a spectrum extracted or summed from an EDS spectrum-image (X-ray map) of an AlSi10Mg alloy fail signal-to-noise or precision checks even for major elements like Al and Si? What total counts or dose are recommended for standard spectra, and is the recommended practice to acquire several long point/raster spectra (e.g. four 60-second acquisitions), check for outliers, and sum them?

Start by making a plan, and update the plan as you go. Your answer will be returned to the user when all plan objectives are completed. Be thorough and ensure your evidence matches the user's question.

Initially useful for qualitative analysis, EDS has developed into a fully quantitative analytical tool that can match wavelength dispersive spectrometry for accuracy in the determination of major (mass concentration C > 0.1) and minor (0.01 ≤ C ≤ 0.1) constituents, and useful accuracy can extend well into the trace (0.001 < C < 0.01) constituent range even when severe peak interference occurs. By recording a full EDS spectrum at each picture element of a scan, comprehensive quantitative compositional mapping can also be performed.

Abstract:
X-ray spectral imaging provides quantitative imaging of trace elements in a biological sample with high sensitivity. We propose a novel algorithm to promote the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) of x-ray spectral images that have low photon counts. Firstly, we estimate the image data area that belongs to the homogeneous parts through confidence interval testing. Then, we apply the Poisson regression through its maximum likelihood estimation on this area to estimate the true photon counts from the Poisson noise corrupted data. Unlike other denoising methods based on regression analysis, we use the bootstrap resampling method to ensure the accuracy of regression estimation. Finally, we use a robust local nonparametric regression method to estimate the baseline and subsequently subtract it from the x-ray spectral data to further improve the SNR of the data. Experiments on several real samples show that the proposed method performs better than some state-of-the-art approaches to ensure accuracy and precision for quantitative analysis of the different trace elements in a standard reference biological sample.

However, the hyperspectral nature of ToF-SIMS datasets can be challenging to analyze and interpret. Both supervised and unsupervised machine learning (ML) approaches are increasingly useful to help analyze ToF-SIMS data. Random Forest (RF) has emerged as a robust and powerful algorithm for processing mass spectrometry data. Abstract:
An unprecedented spectroscopic data stream will soon become available with forthcoming Earth-observing satellite missions equipped with imaging spectroradiometers. This data stream will open up a vast array of opportunities to quantify a diversity of biochemical and structural vegetation properties. The processing requirements for such large data streams require reliable retrieval techniques enabling the spatiotemporally explicit quantification of biophysical variables. With the aim of preparing for this new era of Earth observation, this review summarizes the state-of-the-art retrieval methods that have been applied in experimental imaging spectroscopy studies inferring all kinds of vegetation biophysical variables. Identified retrieval methods are categorized into: (1) parametric regression, including vegetation indices, shape indices and spectral transformations; (2) nonparametric regression, including linear and nonlinear machine learning regression algorithms; (3) physically based, including inversion of radiative transfer models (RTMs) using numerical optimization and look-up table approaches; and (4) hybrid regression methods, which combine RTM simulations with machine learning regression methods. For each of these categories, an overview of widely applied methods with application to mapping vegetation properties is given. In view of processing imaging spectroscopy data, a critical aspect involves the challenge of dealing with spectral multicollinearity. The ability to provide robust estimates, retrieval uncertainties and acceptable retrieval processing speed are other important aspects in view of operational processing. Recommendations towards new-generation spectroscopy-based processing chains for operational production of biophysical variables are given.

A series of fluorophores with single-exponential fluorescence decays in liquid solution at 20 degrees C were measured independently by nine laboratories using single-photon timing and multifrequency phase and modulation fluorometry instruments with lasers as excitation source. The dyes that can serve as fluorescence lifetime standards for time-domain and frequency-domain measurements are all commercially available, are photostable under the conditions of the measurements, and are soluble in solvents of spectroscopic quality (methanol, cyclohexane, water). These lifetime standards are anthracene, 9-cyanoanthracene, 9,10-diphenylanthracene, N-methylcarbazole, coumarin 153, erythrosin B, N-acetyl-l-tryptophanamide, 1,4-bis(5-phenyloxazol-2-yl)benzene, 2,5-diphenyloxazole, rhodamine B, rubrene, N-(3-sulfopropyl)acridinium, and 1,4-diphenylbenzene. The decay times are independent of the excitation and emission wavelengths. Dependent on the structure of the dye and the solvent, the excitation wavelengths used range from 284 to 575 nm, the emission from 330 to 630 nm. These lifetime standards may be used to either calibrate or test the resolution of time- and frequency-domain instrumentation or as reference compounds to eliminate the color effect in photomultiplier tubes. Statistical analyses by means of two-sample charts indicate that there is no laboratory bias in the lifetime determinations. Moreover, statistical tests show that there is an excellent correlation between the lifetimes estimated by the time-domain and frequency-domain fluorometries. Comprehensive tables compiling the results for 20 (fluorescence lifetime standard/solvent) combinations are given.

## pqac-00000000

From text 'newbury2019electronexcitedxraymicroanalysis pages 20-22'.

Dale E. Newbury and Nicholas W.M. Ritchie. Electron-excited x-ray microanalysis by energy dispersive spectrometry at 50: analytical accuracy, precision, trace sensitivity, and quantitative compositional mapping. Microscopy and Microanalysis, 25:1075-1105, Oct 2019. URL: https://doi.org/10.1017/s143192761901482x, doi:10.1017/s143192761901482x. This article has 75 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt provides only limited information relevant to acquiring measured EDS standard spectra and does not state explicit NIST or DTSA-II requirements for total counts, electron dose or current-time product, precision/counting-statistics thresholds, repeated acquisitions, outlier rejection, or summing procedures. It documents that the Th–U peak-fitting test used experimentally measured spectra with very large original family counts: 63,004,000 counts for the Th M family and 58,282,000 for the U M family. The figures identify the spectra as experimentally measured and processed with NIST DTSA-II spectrum tools, but no acquisition protocol is given. For spectrum imaging, the article says that a complete EDS spectrum is recorded at every pixel. In the cited fast-mapping example, the average throughput was 700 kHz and the scan lasted 5 s; however, individual pixel spectra contained only about 10–100 integrated counts. Consequently, the resulting gray-level range is severely limited and the maps can reveal only the most abundant elements. This supports caution in treating spectra extracted from individual pixels as statistically robust standards. The excerpt does not discuss whether summing pixels improves quantitative reliability, nor artifacts or limitations specific to summed spectrum-image spectra beyond the low per-pixel counting statistics.

## pqac-00000001

From text 'newbury2019electronexcitedxraymicroanalysis pages 3-4'.

Dale E. Newbury and Nicholas W.M. Ritchie. Electron-excited x-ray microanalysis by energy dispersive spectrometry at 50: analytical accuracy, precision, trace sensitivity, and quantitative compositional mapping. Microscopy and Microanalysis, 25:1075-1105, Oct 2019. URL: https://doi.org/10.1017/s143192761901482x, doi:10.1017/s143192761901482x. This article has 75 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

This excerpt describes how the NIST authors acquired and processed EDS standard spectra, but it does not specify a required or typical total number of spectrum counts, electron dose, beam current–time product, or a formal counting-statistics/precision threshold for acquiring standards. Spectra were collected using vendor EDS software and exported in the Microscopy Society of America .msa format, then processed with the open-access NIST DTSA-II software. DTSA-II uses multiple-linear-least-squares fitting with measured peak references rather than theoretically modeled references. Pure elements were preferred both as peak-fitting references and compositional standards; when elements were unsuitable because of vacuum incompatibility or beam damage, stable stoichiometric compounds were used. Quantification applied matrix corrections using the Pouchou–Pichoir formulation. The authors emphasize inspecting the raw analytical total before normalization: totals typically fell between 0.98 and 1.02 at 10–20 keV, while a total below unity may indicate an unrecognized or unanalyzed constituent. The excerpt also mentions residual-spectrum inspection for hidden peaks, subject to spectrum statistics. It provides no recommendations here about repeated acquisitions, outlier rejection, summing spectra, or limitations specific to extracted or summed spectrum-image spectra.

Abstract:
A summary of the technical advances that are incorporated in the fourth major release of the Q-Chem quantum chemistry program is provided, covering approximately the last seven years. These include developments in density functional theory methods and algorithms, nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) property evaluation, coupled cluster and perturbation theories, methods for electronically excited and open-shell species, tools for treating extended environments, algorithms for walking on potential surfaces, analysis tools, energy and electron transfer modelling, parallel computing capabilities, and graphical user interfaces. In addition, a selection of example case studies that illustrate these capabilities is given. These include extensive benchmarks of the comparative accuracy of modern density functionals for bonded and non-bonded interactions, tests of attenuated second order Møller–Plesset (MP2) methods for intermolecular interactions, a variety of parallel performance benchmarks, and tests of the accuracy of implicit solvation models. Some specific chemical examples include calculations on the strongly correlated Cr2 dimer, exploring zeolite-catalysed ethane dehydrogenation, energy decomposition analysis of a charged ter-molecular complex arising from glycerol photoionisation, and natural transition orbitals for a Frenkel exciton state in a nine-unit model of a self-assembling nanotube.

Abstract:
The determination of the direction of a stellar core collapse via its neutrino emission is crucial for the identification of the progenitor for a multimessenger follow-up. A highly effective method of reconstructing supernova directions within the Deep Underground Neutrino Experiment (DUNE) is introduced. The supernova neutrino pointing resolution is studied by simulating and reconstructing electron-neutrino charged-current absorption on Ar40 and elastic scattering of neutrinos on electrons. Procedures to reconstruct individual interactions, including a newly developed technique called “brems flipping,” as well as the burst direction from an ensemble of interactions are described. Performance of the burst direction reconstruction is evaluated for supernovae happening at a distance of 10 kpc for a specific supernova burst flux model. The pointing resolution is found to be 3.4 degrees at 68% coverage for a perfect interaction-channel classification and a fiducial mass of 40 kton, and 6.6 degrees for a 10 kton fiducial mass respectively. Assuming a 4% rate of charged-current interactions being misidentified as elastic scattering, DUNE’s burst pointing resolution is found to be 4.3 degrees (8.7 degrees) at 68% coverage.

Abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
        <jats:p>The aim of this study was to explore a new method for changing the flavor of coffee between post harvesting and roasting process. As a preliminary study on the introduction of foreign flavor components, four methods were used to process Kenyan green coffee beans with high water content: drying, freeze-drying, short-time heating puffing, and microwave puffing to modify the structure of green coffee beans. The color change and porosity of the modified green coffee beans were then studied, and the microstructure of the beans was observed using a scanning electron microscopy. The study found that the <jats:italic>ΔE*</jats:italic> value of the modified green coffee beans was lower than 9.47, which is the <jats:italic>ΔE*</jats:italic> value of light-roasted coffee beans. Except for the green coffee beans treated with short-time heating (3 min) puffing, the <jats:italic>ΔE*</jats:italic> value of the modified green coffee beans was lower than 6.53. In addition, coffee beans that underwent short-time heating (1 or 2 min) puffing and microwave puffing had higher porosity and looser microstructure. The green coffee beans with a moisture content of 38.77% had a porosity of 21.77% and 32.64% after being short-time heating (2 min) puffed and microwave puffed, respectively. In conclusion, short-time heating for 1 or 2 puffing and microwave puffing were effective methods for changing the microstructure of green coffee beans.</jats:p>

Abstract:
ABSTRACT Ion Doped Metal Oxide and its Influence on the Power Conversion Efficiency of Perovskite Solar Cells Dwayne Jensen Reddy Doctor of Applied Sciences This study focuses on the fabrication and characterization of Zinc-doped Titanium dioxide (ZnTiO2) as an Electron Transport Layer (ETL) in CH3NH3PbI3-based perovskite solar cells (PSCs). A one-step spin coating technique under controlled ambient conditions (relative humidity < 65%, room temperature ∼ 20oC ) for the development of PSC was applied to investigate the effects of Zn-ion doping on the structural, morphological, optical, and photovoltaic properties. Numerical simulations using SCAPS 1D were additionally performed to further investigate the influence of ion doping on the power conversion efficiency (PCE) of PSCs. Zn-doped TiO2 was successfully incorporated into the TiO2 crystal structure using the solgel technique. Characterization through X-ray diffraction (XRD) and Energy Dispersive X-ray Spectroscopy (EDX) confirmed the incorporation of Zn ions. The crystallite size ranged from 19.99 to 7.1 nm, depending on the Zn ion doping concentration. XRD results also indicate the formation of a highly crystalline tetragonal perovskite (CH3NH3PbI3) phase. Fourier Transform Infrared (FTIR) spectroscopy verified the presence of the anatase phase of Zn-doped TiO2, while the formation of the adduct of Pb2 with dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO) and methylammonium iodide (MAI) was confirmed at 1015 cm-1. Scanning Electron Microscope (SEM) images exhibited fairly smooth and uniform surface coverage for the Zn-doped TiO2 layers. The Root Mean Square (Rq) values for surface roughness showed a decrease from 26.85 nm for undoped TiO2 to 23.4 nm for the 5 mol% Zn-doped TiO2 layer. UV-Vis spectroscopy demonstrated low light transmission loss characteristics from 300 to 790 nm, with the 2 mol% Zn-doped TiO2 showing slightly improved light transmission between 550 and 800 nm. The bandgap energy of undoped and Zn-doped TiO2 ranged from 3.53 to 3.38 eV, while the perovskite layer exhibited a bandgap energy of 2.06 eV. Experimentally, an optimum PCE of 5.67% was achieved with a 2 mol% dopant concentration. However, increasing the Zn dopant to 5 mol% led to a slight deterioration in the PCE. Numerical simulations revealed that increasing the donor doping concentration in the ETL improved the conduction band alignment at the ETL and perovskite interface, resulting in a PCE of 6.17%. Optimizing the absorber acceptor doping concentration and band gap improved the PCE to 10.79%, however, created a pronounced conduction band offset at the ETL/perovskite interface. This was mitigated by introducing an interfacial layer of Cubic Silicon Carbide (3C-SiC) between the absorber and ETL to minimize the conduction band offset, ultimately achieving a PCE of 12.09%.

Abstract:

C Teng. High resolution x-ray imaging and quantitative microanalysis in electron microscopy. Unknown journal, 2020.

The excerpt indicates why an SEM-EDS spectrum image or a summed/region-extracted spectrum may fail precision or signal-to-noise requirements even when Al and Si are major elements. Accurate X-ray mapping requires sufficient characteristic counts to overcome bremsstrahlung; if counts per pixel are low, summing pixels or extracting a region may still provide inadequate statistics for the intended quantitative result, particularly where composition varies spatially. The text emphasizes that acquisition time is the straightforward way to increase counts, but this reduces analytical efficiency. Increasing detector input count rate is also not unlimited: dead time causes the output rate used for maps to diverge from the input rate, because the detector is occupied processing prior photons. Longer processing time can improve electronic noise and energy resolution, but excessive dead time promotes pulse-pileup distortions, potentially compromising peak intensities and element quantification. Conversely, shortening processing time increases output rate but worsens energy resolution and can affect element identification. The excerpt also notes that X-ray generation and emission volumes depend on beam energy and absorption, so spatial heterogeneity and differing interaction volumes can affect region-based spectra. It does not explicitly discuss Poisson variance, specimen drift, or the need for correct live-time/probe-dose metadata, although the count-rate/dead-time discussion supports the importance of recording acquisition conditions accurately.

The excerpt emphasizes that major-element abundance alone does not guarantee reliable quantitative SEM-EDS results.           496                                                                                       Microsc. Microanal. 28 (Suppl 1), 2022
          doi:10.1017/S143192762200263X                                    © Microscopy Society of America 2022

        Strategies for Standardizing EDS Measurements

         Nicholas W. M. Ritchie*

         National Institute of Standards and Technology, Materials Measurement Science Division, Gaithersburg,
      MD, USA.
        * Corresponding author: nicholas.ritchie@nist.gov

        Energy dispersive X-ray spectrometers (EDS) are capable of precise and accurate electron beam
        measurements of composition. However, the optimal strategies for acquiring EDS standards differ from
            its wavelength dispersive cousin. There is a lot more information in an EDS spectrum that can be used to
         evaluate its quality. This information can be used to perform inter-comparisons between multiple spectra
          collected from the same material.

      When collecting an EDS standard, the goal is to create a single spectrum that best represents the material
          in both intensity and shape. The most direct path is not necessarily the best. Rather than measure a single
        spectrum for a long duration τ, it is often better to spend the same instrument time and collect M spectra
        each for a duration τ/M. The M spectra can be compared to one another, and a sum spectrum constructed
        from the subset of the M spectra that are deemed sufficiently similar. Similarity does not guarantee
          optimality. However, similar spectra are more likely to be optimal as there is only one way to measure
         the optimal spectrum and many ways to measure a bad spectrum. This strategy requires a mechanism for
        comparing spectra for similarity that is independent of dose and relative scale.

      EDS measurements are believed to obey the basic assumptions for a Poisson process both in aggregate
        and on a channel-by-channel basis. For large numbers of events, the Poisson distribution approaches the
        Normal distribution with the same variance. Using this information, we can create a metric to compare
          spectra channel-by-channel. The difference of two spectra collected for identical times at the same probe
          current at two points on a homogeneous, flat polished material is bound on the lower end by the limit
        imposed by the Poissonian process. The strategy is therefore to compare each spectrum in a set of M
         nominally identical spectra with the sum of the other M − 1 spectra and give each spectrum a score
        which has a lower bound of approximately 1 when the spectra differ only by Poisson statistics. Such a
         metric is the mean reduced χ2 statistic [1] defined by




        where N is the number of channels,  Sj,i is the number of X-ray events in the i-th channel of the j-th
        spectrum and dj is the probe dose (probe current × live time.) The sum may be over all channels in the
        spectrum or, better yet, those channels representing the informative part of the spectrum (see Table 1).

         Spectra with    scores closer to unity are more similar and more likely to truly represent the ideal
         spectrum. Removing spectra with high scores and recomputing the metric for each remaining spectrum
         allows you to iteratively evaluate a set of spectra until a self-consistent set is found.

         This strategy has been implemented in DTSA-II’s Spectrum Bundler[2] and in NeXLSpectrum’s
        similarity(…) and findsimilar(…) functions [3] (https://github.com/usnistgov/NeXLSpectrum.jl). In





https://doi.org/10.1017/S143192762200263X Published online by Cambridge University Press            Microsc. Microanal. 28 (Suppl 1), 2022                                                                         497


          practice, careful measurements on ideal samples will produce   metrics that are close to unity. Rougher
          surfaces, inhomogeneous samples or surface contamination are the most common reasons that spectra
        have metrics significantly larger than unity. With materials that are truly inhomogeneous, like some
          natural mineral standards, it can be necessary to accept   metrics far from unity.

         In addition, the Duane-Hunt limit [4] should be checked on every measured spectrum. The Duane-Hunt
          limit  is the energy at which the signal from the X-ray continuum goes to zero (see Figure  1.)
         Conservation of energy limits the maximum energy of continuum X-rays to less than the incident
          electron energy. X-rays approaching the incident electron beam energy are increasingly rare, so the
          signal is necessarily small. Regardless, it is possible to fit a continuum model to the last couple thousand
          electronvolts of the continuum signal and in this manner estimate the Duane-Hunt. The estimated
        Duane-Hunt can be compared to the nominal beam energy. Significant disparities should be investigated
         as they may reflect an incident beam energy less than intended (as, for example, sample charging). The
          characteristic  intensity  depends  strongly upon  the  incident beam  energy  (particularly  at low
         overvoltage).

         Spectra that pass both the χ2 ν test and the Duane-Hunt test are likely, when summed, to produce
          representative standards in which you can have a high degree of confidence. EDS spectra can also be
        used in a similar manner as a quality control mechanism when standardizing WDS. Wavelength
        measurements associated with disparate spectra should be considered for culling.

95   for these measurements due to its relative ease of polishing and resistance to oxidation compared to other metals. Beam

120      We observed significant beam current instability if we began analysis immediately after a sample change,

     beam current usually stabilized after 30–60 min. We initially suspected that the additional pumping was required to

      achieve a better vacuum beyond that registered as a “high-vacuum” state by the SEM software, perhaps exacerbated

messages.content:
### Artifact (ID artifact-00)

| Topic | Evidence-based guidance | Interpretation |
|---|---|---|
| NIST formal target | NIST does **not** prescribe one universal count total or acquisition time. It defines probe dose as **beam current × live time** and emphasizes spectral consistency and valid acquisition conditions. (pqac-00000018) | Specify and preserve current, live time, detector conditions, and resulting counts rather than treating “60 s” alone as a sufficient dose specification. |
| Empirical count guidance | Instrument-specific testing found that about **0.5 million total counts** could give **<2% RSD for major elements**; **1–1.5 million** was a practical baseline, with diminishing returns above this range. Counts up to **2.5 million** still improved some minor-element results. (pqac-00000019) | Aim initially for roughly **1–1.5 million recorded total counts per final standard**, then validate on the actual SEM–EDS system; increase toward 2.5 million when minor constituents require it and the specimen tolerates the dose. |
| Replicate workflow | Split the intended total acquisition into multiple nominally identical spectra; compare them with the dose-independent mean reduced **χ²** metric, for which values near **1** indicate differences consistent with Poisson statistics. Check each spectrum’s **Duane–Hunt limit**, reject anomalous spectra iteratively, and sum the consistent subset. (pqac-00000018) | Replicates expose contamination, roughness, inhomogeneity, charging, beam-energy errors, and other failures that a single long spectrum can conceal. |
| Four 60-second acquisitions | **Four × 60 s** is a reasonable implementation of the replicate-and-sum strategy, but it is **not a NIST-mandated recipe**; earlier NIST work suggested approximately **5–10** subdivisions as another implementation. (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000003) | Use four acquisitions only if they produce adequate counts and mutually consistent spectra. Verify current and live time, acceptable dead time/pileup, homogeneous raster placement, absence of drift or contamination, and no beam-induced damage before summing. |


*Table: A compact distinction between formal NIST guidance, empirical count targets, and the recommended replicate-screen-and-sum workflow for measured EDS standards.*

Artifact IDs that may be injected into the answer: [artifact-00]

Context IDs that may be cited: [pqac-00000000, pqac-00000001, pqac-00000002, pqac-00000003, pqac-00000004, pqac-00000005, pqac-00000006, pqac-00000007, pqac-00000008, pqac-00000009, pqac-00000010, pqac-00000011, pqac-00000012, pqac-00000013, pqac-00000014, pqac-00000015, pqac-00000016, pqac-00000017, pqac-00000018, pqac-00000019]

info.name: read_text
info.description:
Given a list of text names, read their contents.

This tool is valuable to read the full contents of specific parts of documents,
complementing the `gather_evidence` tool's indirect approach.
This can be an especially useful tool if `gather_evidence` does not find evidence,
but you think it is very likely that specific documents are still relevant to the question.

text_name_list.description:
A list of up to 10 text names to read.
These text names can be any valid text names retrieved by other tools.
text_name_list.title: Text Name List

info.name: view_images
info.description:
Retrieve images from a document.

Use this tool when you need to see figures, tables, or other visual content.
The tool works by asking a weaker LLM agent to scan through the document, looking for
visual content matching the query you provide. When the agent finds matches, it will
crop the page to the relevant region. It can be tasked to return multiple images,
if desired. Note that the weaker LLM may be worse at *understanding* images than
you, so double-check its conclusions about the returned images. It is also stateless,
i.e. it will not remember what you have asked it to find in the past.

Use this tool carefully. It is difficult to retrieve images, and the images
themselves will fill up your context window quickly. Here are some guidelines:
1. ALWAYS use this tool if the question explicitly mentions 'Table X' or 'Figure Y'.
   These questions require visual content and cannot be answered with text alone.
2. Use this tool as a fallback when gather_evidence fails repeatedly (2+ times
   returning 'No relevant evidence'). This suggests the answer may be in visual content.
3. When gather_evidence returns text mentioning 'see Figure X' or 'shown in Table Y',
   you should call this tool to examine that specific visual reference.
4. Only call this tool after directly inspecting relevant text with read_text
   to confirm the document likely contains the visual you need.
5. Don't use this tool in a broad-spectrum way (don't call on many documents
   just to see what might be relevant).
6. Never call this tool in parallel with itself.
7. Users like visual evidence, so call this tool at least once before answering so you
   can provide some image citations in the answer. Add this to your plan so you do not forget.
   For images to be presented to the user, they must be cited in the final answer after retrieval
   by this tool. You may ignore this instruction if the request is for the question is asking
   for a specific piece of information and is not an open-ended research question.
8. NEVER cite full-page images in your final answer, unless they are full-page panels figures or
   tables. Cite relevant cropped regions if available, otherwise consider calling this tool again
   to find a smaller region that answers the query.

query.description:
Query to search for visual content in the document. If you know the specific
figure/table/formula you are looking for, you can specify it here (e.g. "find me
Figure 3" or "extract the table on page 10"). You can also request based on content
(e.g. "find me all volcano plots of gene X" or "I need the formula for the growth rate").
You can even include explicit instructions for the LLM agent to follow (if helpful, not
necessarily required). The more specific and clear your query is here, the higher the
chance of success.
query.title: Query

text_name.description: Name of a text chunk (e.g., 'smith2023example pages 1-5').
text_name.title: Text Name

info.name: create_artifact
info.description:
Create an artifact that can be used in the final answer, based on information
you have collected so far.

How it works: the full message history thus far is passed to another LLM,
along with the question and your description. The LLM is tasked to create
an artifact that matches your specifications, including a title, caption,
and markdown content. You drive the process by specifying the type and
describing what you want.

Only use this tool *after* you have gathered sufficient evidence or
information to create a new artifact. Do not call this tool in parallel
with tools that are searching for information or evidence that would be
necessary to create this artifact.

It is very helpful after calls to several search tools,
after calls to the `gather_evidence` tool, but it is not required.
However, it should be called before the `answer` tool at
least one time, but more may be given if specifically helpful for
the task, so that the `answer` tool can use the artifacts for the answer.

An artifact can be any string representable fact or list of facts,
formatted using markdown syntax. The artifact will be generated as one of
the following types:
- table: Markdown tables with rows and columns (e.g., findings, methods, molecules)
- code_block: Code snippets in fenced code blocks
- blockquote: Quoted text or important facts (using > prefix)
- image: AI-generated image (chart, diagram, or visualization)

Each artifact consists of:
- A short title (3-8 words) that names what the artifact contains
- A caption (1-2 sentences) describing what the artifact shows and why it's useful
- Markdown content in a single element type (validated automatically with retries if needed)
  For image type, content is a markdown image embed ``![title](data:image/png;base64,...)``,
  embedding the PNG directly as a base64 data URL.

artifact_type.description:
Artifact type to create. Must be one of: table,
code_block, blockquote, image.
artifact_type.title: Artifact Type

description.description:
Description of what you want in the artifact. Be specific
about what information should be included, how it should be organized,
and what columns/sections/content you want. This guides the summary LLM.
For image type, describe the visual you want generated in detail.
description.title: Description

info.name: open_targets_search
info.description:
Search for disease-target associations from OpenTargets database.

Adds new disease-target association data to the state and returns top search results.

List of disease names to search for.
Usage:
disease_names = ["Alzheimer's"] ->
    Returns top targets for Alzheimer's
disease_names = ["Alzheimer's", "Diabetes"], target_names = ["PSEN1"] ->
    Filters for only PSEN1-Alzheimer's/Diabetes evidence

info.name: patent_search
info.description:
Search for patents to increase the patent count.

Repeat previous calls with the same query to continue a search.
Only repeat a maximum of three times.
This tool can be called concurrently.
This tool introduces novel patents, so invoke it when just beginning
or when unsatisfied with the current evidence.

query.description:
A search query for patents (using Google Patents). Never include temporal
filters here (e.g. specific years or dates); instead use the `after` and `before`
arguments. Never include author filters here; instead use the `inventor` argument.
Supports the following syntax, but they can be brittle and are not preferred; try
simple queries where possible:
- Boolean operators: AND (default), OR, and - (NOT)
- Exact phrases: "quoted text"
- Proximity: NEAR/x, ADJ/x (ordered), WITH (20 words), SAME (200 words)
- Field search: TI=(title), AB=(abstract), CL=(claims)
- CPC codes: cpc:A01B or CPC=B60R22/low (includes children)
- Wildcards: ? (0-1 char), * (0+ chars), # (exactly 1 char)
- Chemistry: exact molecule names, SSS=molecule (substructure),
  ~molecule (similar), SMILES strings, SMARTS=pattern, InChI keys,
  CL=~molecule (chemistry in claims)
query.title: Query

after.description:
Minimum patent date. Format: YYYYMMDD.
Example: '20150101' for patents after Jan 1, 2015.
after.title: After

before.description:
Maximum patent date. Format: YYYYMMDD.
Example: '20200101' for patents before Jan 1, 2020.
before.title: Before

date_type.description:
Type of date that after and before refer to. Must be either 'publication'
or 'filing'. Only necessary to set if after and/or before are set.
date_type.title: Date Type

inventor.description: Filter by inventor name(s). Comma-separated for multiple.
inventor.title: Inventor

info.name: clinical_trials_search
info.description:
Search for clinical trials, with support for repeated calls and concurrent execution.

Will add new clinical trials to the state, and return metadata about the number of trials found.

query.description:
The search query string. Supports complex boolean expressions, field-specific
searches, and query modifiers through operators. All configuration is done through
operators in the query string.
Query Syntax:
    Basic Search:
        Simple text automatically uses default EXPANSION[Relaxation] and COVERAGE[Contains]
        >>> "heart attack"

    Modified Search:
        Use operators to modify search behavior:
        >>> 'EXPANSION[None]COVERAGE[FullMatch]"exact phrase"'
        >>> 'EXPANSION[Concept]heart attack'

    Field Search:
        Specify fields using AREA operator:
        >>> 'AREA[InterventionName]aspirin'
        >>> 'AREA[Phase]PHASE3'

    Location Search:
        Use SEARCH operator for compound location queries:
        >>> 'cancer AND SEARCH[Location](AREA[LocationCity]Boston AND AREA[LocationState]Massachusetts)'

    Complex Boolean:
        Combine terms with AND, OR, NOT and parentheses:
        >>> '(cancer OR tumor) AND NOT (EXPANSION[None]pediatric OR AREA[StdAge]CHILD)'

    Date Ranges:
        Use RANGE to specify date ranges with formats like "yyyy-MM" or "yyyy-MM-dd".
        Note that MIN and MAX can be used for open-ended ranges:
        >>> AREA[ResultsFirstPostDate]RANGE[2015-01-01, MAX]

Operators:
    EXPANSION[type]: Controls term expansion
        - None: Exact match only, case and accent sensitive
        - Term: Includes lexical variants (plurals, spellings)
        - Concept: Includes UMLS synonyms
        - Relaxation: Relaxes adjacency requirements (default)
        - Lossy: Allows missing partial terms

    COVERAGE[type]: Controls text matching
        - FullMatch: Must match entire field
        - StartsWith: Must match beginning of field
        - EndsWith: Must match end of field
        - Contains: Must match part of field (default)

    AREA[field]: Specifies field to search
        - See Field Reference for available fields

    SEARCH[type]: Groups field searches
        - Location: Groups location-related fields
        - Study: Groups study-related fields

Usage Notes:
    - All search expressions are implicitly OR expressions
    - Operator precedence (highest to lowest): terms/source operators, NOT/context operators, AND, OR
    - Use quotes for exact phrase matching: "heart attack"
    - Use parentheses for grouping: (heart OR cardiac) AND attack
    - Use backslash to escape operators: \AND
    - Default expansion is EXPANSION[Relaxation]
    - Default coverage is COVERAGE[Contains]

Field Reference:
    High Priority Fields (weight >= 0.8):
        - NCTId (1.0): Trial identifier
        - Acronym (1.0): Study acronym
        - BriefTitle (0.89): Short title

    Medium Priority Fields (0.5-0.79):

info.name: gather_evidence
info.description:
Given a specific question, gather evidence from full-text of documents that have been retrieved by
previous tool calls.

Here is how the tool works: the provided question is posed to all texts retrieved thus far
by other tools. An LLM sees each text independently and is prompted to find information relevant
to the question.

That is, we sample evidence `e \sim LLM(prompt, text, q)` for each text. We only return pieces of
evidence `e` that are sufficiently relevant to the question; if the text is irrelevant, then `e`
is not included in the final response of this tool. Note that this LLM does not see the conversation
history thus far, only the question and each text. Note that it only sees text, no images or other

Abstract 2018 marked the 50th anniversary of the introduction of energy dispersive X-ray spectrometry (EDS) with semiconductor detectors to electron-excited X-ray microanalysis. Initially useful for qualitative analysis, EDS has developed into a fully quantitative analytical tool that can match wavelength dispersive spectrometry for accuracy in the determination of major (mass concentration C > 0.1) and minor (0.01 ≤ C ≤ 0.1) constituents, and useful accuracy can extend well into the trace (0.001 < C < 0.01) constituent range even when severe peak interference occurs. Accurate analysis is possible for low atomic number elements (B, C, N, O, and F), and at low beam energy, which can optimize lateral and depth spatial resolution. By recording a full EDS spectrum at each picture element of a scan, comprehensive quantitative compositional mapping can also be performed.

Abstract:
X-ray spectral imaging provides quantitative imaging of trace elements in a biological sample with high sensitivity. We propose a novel algorithm to promote the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) of x-ray spectral images that have low photon counts. Firstly, we estimate the image data area that belongs to the homogeneous parts through confidence interval testing. Then, we apply the Poisson regression through its maximum likelihood estimation on this area to estimate the true photon counts from the Poisson noise corrupted data. Unlike other denoising methods based on regression analysis, we use the bootstrap resampling method to ensure the accuracy of regression estimation. Finally, we use a robust local nonparametric regression method to estimate the baseline and subsequently subtract it from the x-ray spectral data to further improve the SNR of the data. Experiments on several real samples show that the proposed method performs better than some state-of-the-art approaches to ensure accuracy and precision for quantitative analysis of the different trace elements in a standard reference biological sample.

Abstract:
An unprecedented spectroscopic data stream will soon become available with forthcoming Earth-observing satellite missions equipped with imaging spectroradiometers. This data stream will open up a vast array of opportunities to quantify a diversity of biochemical and structural vegetation properties. The processing requirements for such large data streams require reliable retrieval techniques enabling the spatiotemporally explicit quantification of biophysical variables. With the aim of preparing for this new era of Earth observation, this review summarizes the state-of-the-art retrieval methods that have been applied in experimental imaging spectroscopy studies inferring all kinds of vegetation biophysical variables. Identified retrieval methods are categorized into: (1) parametric regression, including vegetation indices, shape indices and spectral transformations; (2) nonparametric regression, including linear and nonlinear machine learning regression algorithms; (3) physically based, including inversion of radiative transfer models (RTMs) using numerical optimization and look-up table approaches; and (4) hybrid regression methods, which combine RTM simulations with machine learning regression methods. For each of these categories, an overview of widely applied methods with application to mapping vegetation properties is given. In view of processing imaging spectroscopy data, a critical aspect involves the challenge of dealing with spectral multicollinearity. The ability to provide robust estimates, retrieval uncertainties and acceptable retrieval processing speed are other important aspects in view of operational processing. Recommendations towards new-generation spectroscopy-based processing chains for operational production of biophysical variables are given.

Abstract:
A series of fluorophores with single-exponential fluorescence decays in liquid solution at 20 degrees C were measured independently by nine laboratories using single-photon timing and multifrequency phase and modulation fluorometry instruments with lasers as excitation source. The dyes that can serve as fluorescence lifetime standards for time-domain and frequency-domain measurements are all commercially available, are photostable under the conditions of the measurements, and are soluble in solvents of spectroscopic quality (methanol, cyclohexane, water). These lifetime standards are anthracene, 9-cyanoanthracene, 9,10-diphenylanthracene, N-methylcarbazole, coumarin 153, erythrosin B, N-acetyl-l-tryptophanamide, 1,4-bis(5-phenyloxazol-2-yl)benzene, 2,5-diphenyloxazole, rhodamine B, rubrene, N-(3-sulfopropyl)acridinium, and 1,4-diphenylbenzene. At 20 degrees C, the fluorescence lifetimes vary from 89 ps to 31.2 ns, depending on fluorescent dye and solvent, which is a useful range for modern pico- and nanosecond time-domain or mega- to gigahertz frequency-domain instrumentation. The decay times are independent of the excitation and emission wavelengths. Dependent on the structure of the dye and the solvent, the excitation wavelengths used range from 284 to 575 nm, the emission from 330 to 630 nm. These lifetime standards may be used to either calibrate or test the resolution of time- and frequency-domain instrumentation or as reference compounds to eliminate the color effect in photomultiplier tubes. Statistical analyses by means of two-sample charts indicate that there is no laboratory bias in the lifetime determinations. Moreover, statistical tests show that there is an excellent correlation between the lifetimes estimated by the time-domain and frequency-domain fluorometries. Comprehensive tables compiling the results for 20 (fluorescence lifetime standard/solvent) combinations are given.

Most relevant evidence (with ids):

## pqac-00000000

From text 'newbury2019electronexcitedxraymicroanalysis pages 20-22'.

Dale E. Newbury and Nicholas W.M. Ritchie. Electron-excited x-ray microanalysis by energy dispersive spectrometry at 50: analytical accuracy, precision, trace sensitivity, and quantitative compositional mapping. Microscopy and Microanalysis, 25:1075-1105, Oct 2019. URL: https://doi.org/10.1017/s143192761901482x, doi:10.1017/s143192761901482x. This article has 75 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt provides only limited information relevant to acquiring measured EDS standard spectra and does not state explicit NIST or DTSA-II requirements for total counts, electron dose or current-time product, precision/counting-statistics thresholds, repeated acquisitions, outlier rejection, or summing procedures. It documents that the Th–U peak-fitting test used experimentally measured spectra with very large original family counts: 63,004,000 counts for the Th M family and 58,282,000 for the U M family. The figures identify the spectra as experimentally measured and processed with NIST DTSA-II spectrum tools, but no acquisition protocol is given. For spectrum imaging, the article says that a complete EDS spectrum is recorded at every pixel. In the cited fast-mapping example, the average throughput was 700 kHz and the scan lasted 5 s; however, individual pixel spectra contained only about 10–100 integrated counts. Consequently, the resulting gray-level range is severely limited and the maps can reveal only the most abundant elements. This supports caution in treating spectra extracted from individual pixels as statistically robust standards. The excerpt does not discuss whether summing pixels improves quantitative reliability, nor artifacts or limitations specific to summed spectrum-image spectra beyond the low per-pixel counting statistics.

## pqac-00000001

From text 'newbury2019electronexcitedxraymicroanalysis pages 3-4'.

Dale E. Newbury and Nicholas W.M. Ritchie. Electron-excited x-ray microanalysis by energy dispersive spectrometry at 50: analytical accuracy, precision, trace sensitivity, and quantitative compositional mapping. Microscopy and Microanalysis, 25:1075-1105, Oct 2019. URL: https://doi.org/10.1017/s143192761901482x, doi:10.1017/s143192761901482x. This article has 75 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

This excerpt describes how the NIST authors acquired and processed EDS standard spectra, but it does not specify a required or typical total number of spectrum counts, electron dose, beam current–time product, or a formal counting-statistics/precision threshold for acquiring standards. Spectra were collected using vendor EDS software and exported in the Microscopy Society of America .msa format, then processed with the open-access NIST DTSA-II software. DTSA-II uses multiple-linear-least-squares fitting with measured peak references rather than theoretically modeled references. Pure elements were preferred both as peak-fitting references and compositional standards; when elements were unsuitable because of vacuum incompatibility or beam damage, stable stoichiometric compounds were used. Quantification applied matrix corrections using the Pouchou–Pichoir formulation. The authors emphasize inspecting the raw analytical total before normalization: totals typically fell between 0.98 and 1.02 at 10–20 keV, while a total below unity may indicate an unrecognized or unanalyzed constituent. The excerpt also mentions residual-spectrum inspection for hidden peaks, subject to spectrum statistics. It provides no recommendations here about repeated acquisitions, outlier rejection, summing spectra, or limitations specific to extracted or summed spectrum-image spectra.

Abstract:
A summary of the technical advances that are incorporated in the fourth major release of the Q-Chem quantum chemistry program is provided, covering approximately the last seven years. These include developments in density functional theory methods and algorithms, nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) property evaluation, coupled cluster and perturbation theories, methods for electronically excited and open-shell species, tools for treating extended environments, algorithms for walking on potential surfaces, analysis tools, energy and electron transfer modelling, parallel computing capabilities, and graphical user interfaces. In addition, a selection of example case studies that illustrate these capabilities is given. These include extensive benchmarks of the comparative accuracy of modern density functionals for bonded and non-bonded interactions, tests of attenuated second order Møller–Plesset (MP2) methods for intermolecular interactions, a variety of parallel performance benchmarks, and tests of the accuracy of implicit solvation models. Some specific chemical examples include calculations on the strongly correlated Cr2 dimer, exploring zeolite-catalysed ethane dehydrogenation, energy decomposition analysis of a charged ter-molecular complex arising from glycerol photoionisation, and natural transition orbitals for a Frenkel exciton state in a nine-unit model of a self-assembling nanotube.

Abstract:
The determination of the direction of a stellar core collapse via its neutrino emission is crucial for the identification of the progenitor for a multimessenger follow-up. A highly effective method of reconstructing supernova directions within the Deep Underground Neutrino Experiment (DUNE) is introduced. The supernova neutrino pointing resolution is studied by simulating and reconstructing electron-neutrino charged-current absorption on Ar40 and elastic scattering of neutrinos on electrons. Procedures to reconstruct individual interactions, including a newly developed technique called “brems flipping,” as well as the burst direction from an ensemble of interactions are described. Performance of the burst direction reconstruction is evaluated for supernovae happening at a distance of 10 kpc for a specific supernova burst flux model. The pointing resolution is found to be 3.4 degrees at 68% coverage for a perfect interaction-channel classification and a fiducial mass of 40 kton, and 6.6 degrees for a 10 kton fiducial mass respectively. Assuming a 4% rate of charged-current interactions being misidentified as elastic scattering, DUNE’s burst pointing resolution is found to be 4.3 degrees (8.7 degrees) at 68% coverage.

Abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
        <jats:p>The aim of this study was to explore a new method for changing the flavor of coffee between post harvesting and roasting process. As a preliminary study on the introduction of foreign flavor components, four methods were used to process Kenyan green coffee beans with high water content: drying, freeze-drying, short-time heating puffing, and microwave puffing to modify the structure of green coffee beans. The color change and porosity of the modified green coffee beans were then studied, and the microstructure of the beans was observed using a scanning electron microscopy. The study found that the <jats:italic>ΔE*</jats:italic> value of the modified green coffee beans was lower than 9.47, which is the <jats:italic>ΔE*</jats:italic> value of light-roasted coffee beans. Except for the green coffee beans treated with short-time heating (3 min) puffing, the <jats:italic>ΔE*</jats:italic> value of the modified green coffee beans was lower than 6.53. In addition, coffee beans that underwent short-time heating (1 or 2 min) puffing and microwave puffing had higher porosity and looser microstructure. The green coffee beans with a moisture content of 38.77% had a porosity of 21.77% and 32.64% after being short-time heating (2 min) puffed and microwave puffed, respectively. In conclusion, short-time heating for 1 or 2 puffing and microwave puffing were effective methods for changing the microstructure of green coffee beans.</jats:p>

Abstract:
ABSTRACT Ion Doped Metal Oxide and its Influence on the Power Conversion Efficiency of Perovskite Solar Cells Dwayne Jensen Reddy Doctor of Applied Sciences This study focuses on the fabrication and characterization of Zinc-doped Titanium dioxide (ZnTiO2) as an Electron Transport Layer (ETL) in CH3NH3PbI3-based perovskite solar cells (PSCs). A one-step spin coating technique under controlled ambient conditions (relative humidity < 65%, room temperature ∼ 20oC ) for the development of PSC was applied to investigate the effects of Zn-ion doping on the structural, morphological, optical, and photovoltaic properties. Numerical simulations using SCAPS 1D were additionally performed to further investigate the influence of ion doping on the power conversion efficiency (PCE) of PSCs. Zn-doped TiO2 was successfully incorporated into the TiO2 crystal structure using the solgel technique. Characterization through X-ray diffraction (XRD) and Energy Dispersive X-ray Spectroscopy (EDX) confirmed the incorporation of Zn ions. The crystallite size ranged from 19.99 to 7.1 nm, depending on the Zn ion doping concentration. XRD results also indicate the formation of a highly crystalline tetragonal perovskite (CH3NH3PbI3) phase. Fourier Transform Infrared (FTIR) spectroscopy verified the presence of the anatase phase of Zn-doped TiO2, while the formation of the adduct of Pb2 with dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO) and methylammonium iodide (MAI) was confirmed at 1015 cm-1. Scanning Electron Microscope (SEM) images exhibited fairly smooth and uniform surface coverage for the Zn-doped TiO2 layers. The Root Mean Square (Rq) values for surface roughness showed a decrease from 26.85 nm for undoped TiO2 to 23.4 nm for the 5 mol% Zn-doped TiO2 layer. UV-Vis spectroscopy demonstrated low light transmission loss characteristics from 300 to 790 nm, with the 2 mol% Zn-doped TiO2 showing slightly improved light transmission between 550 and 800 nm. The bandgap energy of undoped and Zn-doped TiO2 ranged from 3.53 to 3.38 eV, while the perovskite layer exhibited a bandgap energy of 2.06 eV. Experimentally, an optimum PCE of 5.67% was achieved with a 2 mol% dopant concentration. However, increasing the Zn dopant to 5 mol% led to a slight deterioration in the PCE. Numerical simulations revealed that increasing the donor doping concentration in the ETL improved the conduction band alignment at the ETL and perovskite interface, resulting in a PCE of 6.17%. Optimizing the absorber acceptor doping concentration and band gap improved the PCE to 10.79%, however, created a pronounced conduction band offset at the ETL/perovskite interface. This was mitigated by introducing an interfacial layer of Cubic Silicon Carbide (3C-SiC) between the absorber and ETL to minimize the conduction band offset, ultimately achieving a PCE of 12.09%.

It is a great time to be a microanalyst. After a few decades of incremental progress in energy-dispersive X-ray spectrometry (EDS), the last decade has seen the accuracy and precision surge forward. Today, the question is not whether EDS is generally useful but to identify the types of problems for which wavelength-dispersive X-ray spectrometry remains the better choice.
