## pqac-00000002

From text 'ritchie2022strategiesforstandardizing pages 1-3'.

Nicholas W M Ritchie. Strategies for standardizing eds measurements. Aug 2022. URL: https://doi.org/10.1017/s143192762200263x, doi:10.1017/s143192762200263x. This article has 1 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt recommends distributing the intended total acquisition time across M nominally identical replicate spectra, each acquired for τ/M, rather than collecting one spectrum for the entire duration τ. The text does not specify a fixed value for M, a target dose, or a target number of counts; it only defines probe dose as probe current × live time and says the same total instrument time should be used. Replicates should be compared with a dose- and scale-independent mean reduced χ² metric. A score near 1 is the expected lower limit when differences are explained by Poisson counting statistics; larger scores identify spectra that are less consistent. High-scoring spectra should be removed, the metric recalculated iteratively, and a self-consistent subset retained. The retained spectra may then be summed to form the standard. Every spectrum should also be checked using the Duane–Hunt limit, and only spectra passing both tests are expected to yield a representative summed standard. The excerpt motivates this approach because one long acquisition cannot provide replicate-to-replicate quality comparisons. It does not specifically discuss why a spectrum-image sum is unsuitable, nor does it provide a prescribed count target.

Rather than collecting one long spectrum with total live time t from a standard, it recommends collecting approximately 5–10 separate spectra, each with live time t/N, so the total acquisition time remains t. The replicate spectra should be compared with one another, allowing anomalous spectra to be rejected. The remaining, mutually consistent spectra should then be summed into one spectrum, which is expected to have high quality. Repeated measurements of unknowns additionally support homogeneity testing and can reveal sample-preparation or metrology problems. The excerpt does not specify the 2022 article’s exact dose or count target, quantitative similarity/outlier criterion, or the precise replicate duration beyond the general t/N rule. Thus, the passage supports the general rationale for segmented acquisitions—detecting outliers and acquisition problems before summing—rather than the exact acquisition parameters requested.

The excerpt documents high-quality volcanic-phase SEM-EDS spectra primarily in the approximately 0.25×10^6–1.5×10^6 total-count range. Standard-condition measurements used about 3 nA beam current, 15 kV, 16 µs process time, and 1.5×10^6 counts. For the beam-sensitive Sheep Track tephra, the optimized protocol used about 3.2 nA with a 5 s live time, producing approximately 0.25×10^6 counts; this gave a mean Na2O of 8.05 wt.% versus an expected 8.19 wt.%, although precision for minor elements was degraded. A comparable 3–3.2 nA, 5 s acquisition corresponds to roughly 15–16 nA·s of current-time exposure. The excerpt also reports lower-current tests at 0.6 nA using repeated 10 s or approximately 27 s acquisitions, and Lipari tests spanning 0.6–12.4 nA with 160–15 s analysis times. For literature context, Guyett et al. estimated detection limits using 1×10^6-count spectra, whereas Newbury and Ritchie used an exceptionally large 87×10^6-count spectrum. The excerpt states that detection limits improve with increasing counts, but it does not identify a count threshold above which precision stopped improving.         Strategies for Standardizing EDS Measurements

         Nicholas W. M. Ritchie*

         National Institute of Standards and Technology, Materials Measurement Science Division, Gaithersburg,
      MD, USA.
        * Corresponding author: nicholas.ritchie@nist.gov

        Energy dispersive X-ray spectrometers (EDS) are capable of precise and accurate electron beam
        measurements of composition. However, the optimal strategies for acquiring EDS standards differ from
            its wavelength dispersive cousin. There is a lot more information in an EDS spectrum that can be used to
         evaluate its quality. This information can be used to perform inter-comparisons between multiple spectra
          collected from the same material.

      When collecting an EDS standard, the goal is to create a single spectrum that best represents the material
          in both intensity and shape. The most direct path is not necessarily the best. Rather than measure a single
        spectrum for a long duration τ, it is often better to spend the same instrument time and collect M spectra
        each for a duration τ/M. The M spectra can be compared to one another, and a sum spectrum constructed
        from the subset of the M spectra that are deemed sufficiently similar. Similarity does not guarantee
          optimality. However, similar spectra are more likely to be optimal as there is only one way to measure
         the optimal spectrum and many ways to measure a bad spectrum. This strategy requires a mechanism for
        comparing spectra for similarity that is independent of dose and relative scale.

      EDS measurements are believed to obey the basic assumptions for a Poisson process both in aggregate
        and on a channel-by-channel basis. For large numbers of events, the Poisson distribution approaches the
        Normal distribution with the same variance. Using this information, we can create a metric to compare
          spectra channel-by-channel. The difference of two spectra collected for identical times at the same probe
          current at two points on a homogeneous, flat polished material is bound on the lower end by the limit
        imposed by the Poissonian process. The strategy is therefore to compare each spectrum in a set of M
         nominally identical spectra with the sum of the other M − 1 spectra and give each spectrum a score
        which has a lower bound of approximately 1 when the spectra differ only by Poisson statistics. Such a
         metric is the mean reduced χ2 statistic [1] defined by




        where N is the number of channels,  Sj,i is the number of X-ray events in the i-th channel of the j-th
        spectrum and dj is the probe dose (probe current × live time.) The sum may be over all channels in the
        spectrum or, better yet, those channels representing the informative part of the spectrum (see Table 1).

         Spectra with    scores closer to unity are more similar and more likely to truly represent the ideal
         spectrum. Removing spectra with high scores and recomputing the metric for each remaining spectrum
         allows you to iteratively evaluate a set of spectra until a self-consistent set is found.

         This strategy has been implemented in DTSA-II’s Spectrum Bundler[2] and in NeXLSpectrum’s
        similarity(…) and findsimilar(…) functions [3] (https://github.com/usnistgov/NeXLSpectrum.jl). In

          surfaces, inhomogeneous samples or surface contamination are the most common reasons that spectra
        have metrics significantly larger than unity. With materials that are truly inhomogeneous, like some
          natural mineral standards, it can be necessary to accept   metrics far from unity.

         In addition, the Duane-Hunt limit [4] should be checked on every measured spectrum. The Duane-Hunt
          limit  is the energy at which the signal from the X-ray continuum goes to zero (see Figure  1.)
         Conservation of energy limits the maximum energy of continuum X-rays to less than the incident

100  comparing the Co count rates. The recent installation of a probe current detector has allowed us to retroactively

      calculate the beam current for past analytical sessions based on the Co count rate. Our typical analytical set up for

      minerals uses a current of 2–3 nA.

       calibration is stable for all elements for at least three days, and some elements were stable for months, though we did

105  not systematically investigate the relative calibration stability of different elements. Whereas this report includes only

      standard analysis, for an analysis session including unknowns, three replicates of secondary verification standards are

      run following calibration and at the start of each day if utilizing a previous day’s calibration; in either case additional

       replicates are run throughout the day to monitor the stability of the calibration. Typically, a total of 6–10 analyses will

     be measured daily for each secondary standard. We prefer to reserve our closest matrix-matched standards for

110  secondary verification rather than utilizing them for calibration (supplementary table S1). A summary of the

      considerations and our suggestions for developing a SEM-EDS procedure are in the appendix.

115   figures presented in the text, tables summarizing the results of each test are available in the supplementary materials

      labradorite and chromium augite and MAC olivine standards, except as noted. Throughout this report, results are

      reported as unnormalized wt. % oxides calculated using stoichiometric oxygen, unless otherwise stated.

120      We observed significant beam current instability if we began analysis immediately after a sample change,

     beam current usually stabilized after 30–60 min. We initially suspected that the additional pumping was required to

      achieve a better vacuum beyond that registered as a “high-vacuum” state by the SEM software, perhaps exacerbated

125  by the large sample chamber of our SEM. However, the Tescan MIRA field emission source SEM at the USGS Alaska

      source of the CVO SEM vents during sample exchanges whereas the source of the AVO SEM is maintained at high

130  vacuum. Accordingly, in addition to differences between the source type, we infer that venting, and potentially

      subsequent outgassing of the filament, is the most substantial contributor to the extra pumping and filament warm-up

      time required by the CVO SEM. Accordingly, we expect that the beam stability will vary, perhaps significantly,

135  have not found any other effect of filament age on the performance of the method. We aim to tune the source power,

Include: NIST formal target (no universal count/time; dose=current\u00d7live time); empirical count guidance (~0.5 million may achieve <2% RSD for majors, practical baseline 1\u20131.5 million, diminishing returns after that, up to 2.5 million for minors); replicate workflow (split total time, compare reduced chi-square near 1, Duane-Hunt check, reject outliers, sum retained spectra); four 60-second acquisitions (reasonable but not mandated; verify counts, current, dead time, homogeneity and damage)."}
function.name: create_artifact

messages.content:
### Artifact (ID artifact-00)

| Topic | Evidence-based guidance | Interpretation |
|---|---|---|
| NIST formal target | NIST does **not** prescribe one universal count total or acquisition time. It defines probe dose as **beam current × live time** and emphasizes spectral consistency and valid acquisition conditions. (pqac-00000018) | Specify and preserve current, live time, detector conditions, and resulting counts rather than treating “60 s” alone as a sufficient dose specification. |
| Empirical count guidance | Instrument-specific testing found that about **0.5 million total counts** could give **<2% RSD for major elements**; **1–1.5 million** was a practical baseline, with diminishing returns above this range. Counts up to **2.5 million** still improved some minor-element results. (pqac-00000019) | Aim initially for roughly **1–1.5 million recorded total counts per final standard**, then validate on the actual SEM–EDS system; increase toward 2.5 million when minor constituents require it and the specimen tolerates the dose. |
| Replicate workflow | Split the intended total acquisition into multiple nominally identical spectra; compare them with the dose-independent mean reduced **χ²** metric, for which values near **1** indicate differences consistent with Poisson statistics. Check each spectrum’s **Duane–Hunt limit**, reject anomalous spectra iteratively, and sum the consistent subset. (pqac-00000018) | Replicates expose contamination, roughness, inhomogeneity, charging, beam-energy errors, and other failures that a single long spectrum can conceal. |
| Four 60-second acquisitions | **Four × 60 s** is a reasonable implementation of the replicate-and-sum strategy, but it is **not a NIST-mandated recipe**; earlier NIST work suggested approximately **5–10** subdivisions as another implementation. (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000003) | Use four acquisitions only if they produce adequate counts and mutually consistent spectra. Verify current and live time, acceptable dead time/pileup, homogeneous raster placement, absence of drift or contamination, and no beam-induced damage before summing. |

Why would a spectrum extracted or summed from an EDS spectrum-image (X-ray map) of an AlSi10Mg alloy fail signal-to-noise or precision checks even for major elements like Al and Si? What total counts or dose are recommended for standard spectra, and is the recommended practice to acquire several long point/raster spectra (e.g. four 60-second acquisitions), check for outliers, and sum them?
answer.answer:
## Conclusion

Yes. A spectrum summed or extracted from an AlSi10Mg spectrum-image can fail DTSA-II quality checks even though Al and Si are major constituents, because **major concentration is not equivalent to adequate counting statistics or a valid standard measurement**. The relevant quantities are the recorded counts—especially net characteristic counts above continuum—in a spectrum acquired with known dose, stable conditions, and representative geometry.

### Why a map-derived spectrum can fail

1. **Spectrum-images are commonly dose-starved.** Mapping divides the available dose among many pixels with short dwell times. A NIST example contained only about **10–100 integrated counts per pixel**, enough for fast visualization of abundant elements but severely limiting gray-level and spectral statistics. An extracted region may therefore still contain too few total or net peak counts for reliable background subtraction and peak fitting. Summing does not manufacture information; Poisson relative uncertainty scales approximately as \(1/\sqrt{N}\). (newbury2019electronexcitedxraymicroanalysis pages 20-22)

2. **The continuum and fitting uncertainty still matter.** DTSA-II fits measured peak shapes against the characteristic signal plus bremsstrahlung background. Even a visually prominent Al or Si peak may have inadequate *net* counts, or enough background covariance, to fail a requested precision threshold. Quantitative EDS requires statistically sufficient counts for background subtraction and composition calculation. (teng2020highresolutionxraya pages 21-27, ritchie2018exploringthelimits pages 1-4)

3. **AlSi10Mg is heterogeneous.** A map may combine an Al-rich matrix, Si-rich eutectic/particles, Mg-bearing regions, pores, oxide, contamination, edges, or relief. The sum is then an area-weighted mixture rather than a spectrum of one homogeneous standard composition. Composition-dependent matrix corrections and varying take-off geometry make indiscriminate summation particularly problematic. NIST identifies roughness, inhomogeneity, and surface contamination as common reasons nominal replicate spectra disagree beyond Poisson statistics. (teng2020highresolutionxraya pages 21-27, ritchie2022strategiesforstandardizing pages 1-3)

4. **A hyperspectral sum may carry acquisition defects.** Drift, changing illuminated phases, beam-current instability, charging, contamination growth, detector dead time, and pileup can change spectrum shape or intensity during a map. At high count rate, coincidence events can produce sum peaks and correction artifacts; reliable standards also require correct beam-current/live-time information because intensity scales with dose only while other conditions remain constant. (newbury2019electronexcitedxraymicroanalysis pages 28-29, teng2020highresolutionxraya pages 27-31)

5. **Metadata can be unsuitable after extraction/export.** NIST defines probe dose as **probe current × live time**. If an extracted map spectrum has missing, ambiguous, or incorrectly aggregated live-time/current metadata, DTSA-II cannot reliably normalize it as a measured standard. The displayed map duration or total counts over the entire cube is not necessarily the effective dose for the selected region. (ritchie2018exploringthelimits pages 1-4, ritchie2022strategiesforstandardizing pages 1-3)

Thus, the problem is not that DTSA-II “does not recognize” strong Al and Si peaks. It is that the spectrum may not support the required statistical precision, may not represent one homogeneous material, or may lack trustworthy dose and acquisition information.

## Counts and dose

NIST’s standardization paper does **not prescribe one universal total-count target, acquisition time, or current–time dose**. It emphasizes known probe dose, spectral consistency, and acquisition validity. Acquisition time alone is not transferable between instruments because recorded counts depend on current, detector solid angle and efficiency, processing time, dead time, geometry, and composition. (ritchie2022strategiesforstandardizing pages 1-3)

A useful empirical benchmark from a quantitative SEM–EDS validation study is:

- approximately **0.5 × 10⁶ total counts** could give major-element precision below 2% RSD under that system’s conditions;
- approximately **1–1.5 × 10⁶ total recorded counts** was the practical baseline;
- diminishing returns generally began beyond **1–1.5 × 10⁶**, although increasing toward **2.5 × 10⁶** continued to help some minor constituents;
- its 1.5-million-count baseline was obtained in about 35 s live time at 2.2 nA, corresponding to about **77 nA·s = 77 nC** incident charge, but this is an instrument-specific example—not a universal DTSA-II dose requirement. (andersenUnknownyearascanningelectron pages 4-6)

| Topic | Evidence-based guidance | Interpretation |
|---|---|---|
| NIST formal target | NIST does **not** prescribe one universal count total or acquisition time. It defines probe dose as **beam current × live time** and emphasizes spectral consistency and valid acquisition conditions. (ritchie2022strategiesforstandardizing pages 1-3) | Specify and preserve current, live time, detector conditions, and resulting counts rather than treating “60 s” alone as a sufficient dose specification. |
| Empirical count guidance | Instrument-specific testing found that about **0.5 million total counts** could give **<2% RSD for major elements**; **1–1.5 million** was a practical baseline, with diminishing returns above this range. Counts up to **2.5 million** still improved some minor-element results. (andersenUnknownyearascanningelectron pages 4-6) | Aim initially for roughly **1–1.5 million recorded total counts per final standard**, then validate on the actual SEM–EDS system; increase toward 2.5 million when minor constituents require it and the specimen tolerates the dose. |
| Replicate workflow | Split the intended total acquisition into multiple nominally identical spectra; compare them with the dose-independent mean reduced **χ²** metric, for which values near **1** indicate differences consistent with Poisson statistics. Check each spectrum’s **Duane–Hunt limit**, reject anomalous spectra iteratively, and sum the consistent subset. (ritchie2022strategiesforstandardizing pages 1-3) | Replicates expose contamination, roughness, inhomogeneity, charging, beam-energy errors, and other failures that a single long spectrum can conceal. |
| Four 60-second acquisitions | **Four × 60 s** is a reasonable implementation of the replicate-and-sum strategy, but it is **not a NIST-mandated recipe**; earlier NIST work suggested approximately **5–10** subdivisions as another implementation. (ritchie2022strategiesforstandardizing pages 1-3, ritchie2018exploringthelimits pages 4-5) | Use four acquisitions only if they produce adequate counts and mutually consistent spectra. Verify current and live time, acceptable dead time/pileup, homogeneous raster placement, absence of drift or contamination, and no beam-induced damage before summing. |


*Table: A compact distinction between formal NIST guidance, empirical count targets, and the recommended replicate-screen-and-sum workflow for measured EDS standards.*

## Recommended acquisition practice

The recommended NIST strategy is indeed to acquire **multiple nominally identical point or small-raster spectra**, rather than one uninterrupted long spectrum. Divide total intended time \(\tau\) among \(M\) acquisitions of approximately \(\tau/M\), compare them, reject anomalous members, and sum only the self-consistent subset. DTSA-II’s Spectrum Bundler implements this concept. NIST uses a dose-independent mean reduced-\(\chi^2\) comparison: values near unity indicate differences consistent with Poisson counting statistics; high-scoring spectra are removed iteratively. Every candidate should also pass a Duane–Hunt-limit check for beam-energy/charging problems. (ritchie2022strategiesforstandardizing pages 1-3)

Earlier NIST work suggested approximately **5–10 subdivisions**, but the principle—not a fixed replicate number—is important. (ritchie2018exploringthelimits pages 4-5)

Therefore, **four 60-s point/raster acquisitions, outlier checking, and summing are reasonable practice**, but “4 × 60 s” is not a NIST-prescribed recipe. It is appropriate only if:

- the retained sum reaches adequate recorded counts—practically, often around **1–1.5 million or more**;
- all spectra were collected at the same beam energy, geometry, detector settings, and controlled probe current;
- dead time and pileup remain acceptable;
- the raster lies wholly within a flat, homogeneous region representing the intended standard;
- no charging, drift, contamination, oxidation, or beam-induced compositional change occurs;
- individual live times/doses are correctly preserved and combined; and
- replicate spectra agree statistically before summation.

For heterogeneous AlSi10Mg, a bulk alloy spectrum is generally not an ideal element-specific measured standard unless its composition and homogeneity at the interaction-volume/raster scale are established. Pure Al, pure Si, or certified homogeneous compounds/alloys are preferable measured references; NIST authors prefer pure elements where practical and stable stoichiometric compounds when elemental standards are unsuitable. (newbury2019electronexcitedxraymicroanalysis pages 3-4)

contexts.context: This excerpt describes how the NIST authors acquired and processed EDS standard spectra, but it does not specify a required or typical total number of spectrum counts, electron dose, beam current–time product, or a formal counting-statistics/precision threshold for acquiring standards. Spectra were collected using vendor EDS software and exported in the Microscopy Society of America .msa format, then processed with the open-access NIST DTSA-II software. DTSA-II uses multiple-linear-least-squares fitting with measured peak references rather than theoretically modeled references. Pure elements were preferred both as peak-fitting references and compositional standards; when elements were unsuitable because of vacuum incompatibility or beam damage, stable stoichiometric compounds were used. Quantification applied matrix corrections using the Pouchou–Pichoir formulation. The authors emphasize inspecting the raw analytical total before normalization: totals typically fell between 0.98 and 1.02 at 10–20 keV, while a total below unity may indicate an unrecognized or unanalyzed constituent. The excerpt also mentions residual-spectrum inspection for hidden peaks, subject to spectrum statistics. It provides no recommendations here about repeated acquisitions, outlier rejection, summing spectra, or limitations specific to extracted or summed spectrum-image spectra.
contexts.question: What do NIST authors or DTSA-II documentation recommend for acquiring measured EDS standard spectra: required or typical total spectrum counts, electron dose/current-time product, precision/counting-statistics criteria, and repeated acquisitions/outlier checks/summing? Also explain limitations of extracted or summed spectrum-image spectra.

contexts.context: This excerpt establishes the general NIST authors’ framework for measured EDS standards but does not provide the requested operational acquisition numbers. Standards-based quantification requires measuring the same characteristic peak in the unknown and standard under identical excitation conditions, followed by iterative matrix corrections. The text emphasizes controlling dose, spectrometer performance, and instrumental drift, since these affect analytical totals and elemental determinations. It notes that the raw concentration total is normally not exactly unity because of intensity and matrix-correction uncertainties, typically falling between 0.98 and 1.02; values outside that range should be investigated. Rather than collecting one long spectrum with total live time t from a standard, it recommends collecting approximately 5–10 separate spectra, each with live time t/N, so the total acquisition time remains t. contexts.context: The excerpt does not contain Nicholas Ritchie’s 2022 “Strategies for Standardizing EDS Measurements” or the requested exact acquisition protocol, similarity/outlier criterion, or summing recommendation. It does provide related guidance on EDS acquisition and replication: increasing total spectrum counts improves accuracy and precision but lengthens analysis and may worsen beam damage, with significant diminishing returns reported beyond 1.5 × 10^6 total spectrum counts for most elements. Standards should be analyzed alongside unknowns to monitor drift; secondary standards should be measured at least at the beginning and end of an analytical session, with the authors typically collecting 6–8 replicates per standard per day. For beam-sensitive glass and minerals, raster acquisition can mitigate damage and Na mobility, with 10 µm square rasters effective for many volcanic-glass standards. The excerpt also recommends testing a range of raster sizes and checking whether mobile-element concentrations converge. These points may help contextualize why a single long acquisition could be problematic, but the passage itself does not discuss one-long-spectrum versus summed-spectrum-image strategies, nor does it state the exact dose target, replicate duration, or outlier threshold asked about.

contexts.context: The excerpt recommends distributing the intended total acquisition time across M nominally identical replicate spectra, each acquired for τ/M, rather than collecting one spectrum for the entire duration τ. The text does not specify a fixed value for M, a target dose, or a target number of counts; it only defines probe dose as probe current × live time and says the same total instrument time should be used. Replicates should be compared with a dose- and scale-independent mean reduced χ² metric. A score near 1 is the expected lower limit when differences are explained by Poisson counting statistics; larger scores identify spectra that are less consistent. High-scoring spectra should be removed, the metric recalculated iteratively, and a self-consistent subset retained. The retained spectra may then be summed to form the standard. Every spectrum should also be checked using the Duane–Hunt limit, and only spectra passing both tests are expected to yield a representative summed standard. The excerpt motivates this approach because one long acquisition cannot provide replicate-to-replicate quality comparisons. It does not specifically discuss why a spectrum-image sum is unsuitable, nor does it provide a prescribed count target.

contexts.context: The excerpt documents high-quality volcanic-phase SEM-EDS spectra primarily in the approximately 0.25×10^6–1.5×10^6 total-count range. Standard-condition measurements used about 3 nA beam current, 15 kV, 16 µs process time, and 1.5×10^6 counts. For the beam-sensitive Sheep Track tephra, the optimized protocol used about 3.2 nA with a 5 s live time, producing approximately 0.25×10^6 counts; this gave a mean Na2O of 8.05 wt.% versus an expected 8.19 wt.%, although precision for minor elements was degraded. A comparable 3–3.2 nA, 5 s acquisition corresponds to roughly 15–16 nA·s of current-time exposure. The excerpt also reports lower-current tests at 0.6 nA using repeated 10 s or approximately 27 s acquisitions, and Lipari tests spanning 0.6–12.4 nA with 160–15 s analysis times. For literature context, Guyett et al. estimated detection limits using 1×10^6-count spectra, whereas Newbury and Ritchie used an exceptionally large 87×10^6-count spectrum. The excerpt states that detection limits improve with increasing counts, but it does not identify a count threshold above which precision stopped improving. It instead indicates that short, sufficiently counted acquisitions are preferred for minimizing Na loss.

contexts.context: The excerpt reports testing total spectrum counts from 0.25–2.5 × 10^6 counts. For major elements, acceptable precision (RSD <2%) was achievable at approximately 0.5 × 10^6 counts, whereas minor elements performed poorly below 1 × 10^6 counts, with RSD >40%. Precision improved with increasing counts, but diminishing returns generally began above 1–1.5 × 10^6 counts; some minor-element measurements still benefited from increasing counts to 2.5 × 10^6. The recommended baseline was 1.5 × 10^6 total counts, normally obtained using 35 s live time under conditions of 15 kV accelerating voltage, 2.2 nA beam current, 45–55% dead time, and 16 µs process time. answer.formatted_answer:
Question: In NIST DTSA-II, creating a quantification standard from a measured EDS spectrum requires adequate counting statistics. Why would a spectrum extracted or summed from an EDS spectrum-image (X-ray map) of an AlSi10Mg alloy fail signal-to-noise or precision checks even for major elements like Al and Si? What total counts or dose are recommended for standard spectra, and is the recommended practice to acquire several long point/raster spectra (e.g. four 60-second acquisitions), check for outliers, and sum them?

## Conclusion

Yes. A spectrum summed or extracted from an AlSi10Mg spectrum-image can fail DTSA-II quality checks even though Al and Si are major constituents, because **major concentration is not equivalent to adequate counting statistics or a valid standard measurement**. The relevant quantities are the recorded counts—especially net characteristic counts above continuum—in a spectrum acquired with known dose, stable conditions, and representative geometry.

### Why a map-derived spectrum can fail

1. **Spectrum-images are commonly dose-starved.** Mapping divides the available dose among many pixels with short dwell times. A NIST example contained only about **10–100 integrated counts per pixel**, enough for fast visualization of abundant elements but severely limiting gray-level and spectral statistics. An extracted region may therefore still contain too few total or net peak counts for reliable background subtraction and peak fitting. Summing does not manufacture information; Poisson relative uncertainty scales approximately as \(1/\sqrt{N}\). (newbury2019electronexcitedxraymicroanalysis pages 20-22)

2. **The continuum and fitting uncertainty still matter.** DTSA-II fits measured peak shapes against the characteristic signal plus bremsstrahlung background. Even a visually prominent Al or Si peak may have inadequate *net* counts, or enough background covariance, to fail a requested precision threshold. Quantitative EDS requires statistically sufficient counts for background subtraction and composition calculation. (teng2020highresolutionxraya pages 21-27, ritchie2018exploringthelimits pages 1-4)

3. **AlSi10Mg is heterogeneous.** A map may combine an Al-rich matrix, Si-rich eutectic/particles, Mg-bearing regions, pores, oxide, contamination, edges, or relief. The sum is then an area-weighted mixture rather than a spectrum of one homogeneous standard composition. Composition-dependent matrix corrections and varying take-off geometry make indiscriminate summation particularly problematic. NIST identifies roughness, inhomogeneity, and surface contamination as common reasons nominal replicate spectra disagree beyond Poisson statistics. (teng2020highresolutionxraya pages 21-27, ritchie2022strategiesforstandardizing pages 1-3)

4. **A hyperspectral sum may carry acquisition defects.** Drift, changing illuminated phases, beam-current instability, charging, contamination growth, detector dead time, and pileup can change spectrum shape or intensity during a map. At high count rate, coincidence events can produce sum peaks and correction artifacts; reliable standards also require correct beam-current/live-time information because intensity scales with dose only while other conditions remain constant. (newbury2019electronexcitedxraymicroanalysis pages 28-29, teng2020highresolutionxraya pages 27-31)

5. **Metadata can be unsuitable after extraction/export.** NIST defines probe dose as **probe current × live time**. If an extracted map spectrum has missing, ambiguous, or incorrectly aggregated live-time/current metadata, DTSA-II cannot reliably normalize it as a measured standard. The displayed map duration or total counts over the entire cube is not necessarily the effective dose for the selected region. (ritchie2018exploringthelimits pages 1-4, ritchie2022strategiesforstandardizing pages 1-3)

Thus, the problem is not that DTSA-II “does not recognize” strong Al and Si peaks. It is that the spectrum may not support the required statistical precision, may not represent one homogeneous material, or may lack trustworthy dose and acquisition information.

## Counts and dose

NIST’s standardization paper does **not prescribe one universal total-count target, acquisition time, or current–time dose**. It emphasizes known probe dose, spectral consistency, and acquisition validity. Acquisition time alone is not transferable between instruments because recorded counts depend on current, detector solid angle and efficiency, processing time, dead time, geometry, and composition. (ritchie2022strategiesforstandardizing pages 1-3)

A useful empirical benchmark from a quantitative SEM–EDS validation study is:

- approximately **0.5 × 10⁶ total counts** could give major-element precision below 2% RSD under that system’s conditions;
- approximately **1–1.5 × 10⁶ total recorded counts** was the practical baseline;
- diminishing returns generally began beyond **1–1.5 × 10⁶**, although increasing toward **2.5 × 10⁶** continued to help some minor constituents;
- its 1.5-million-count baseline was obtained in about 35 s live time at 2.2 nA, corresponding to about **77 nA·s = 77 nC** incident charge, but this is an instrument-specific example—not a universal DTSA-II dose requirement. (andersenUnknownyearascanningelectron pages 4-6)

| Topic | Evidence-based guidance | Interpretation |
|---|---|---|
| NIST formal target | NIST does **not** prescribe one universal count total or acquisition time. It defines probe dose as **beam current × live time** and emphasizes spectral consistency and valid acquisition conditions. (ritchie2022strategiesforstandardizing pages 1-3) | Specify and preserve current, live time, detector conditions, and resulting counts rather than treating “60 s” alone as a sufficient dose specification. |
| Empirical count guidance | Instrument-specific testing found that about **0.5 million total counts** could give **<2% RSD for major elements**; **1–1.5 million** was a practical baseline, with diminishing returns above this range. Counts up to **2.5 million** still improved some minor-element results. (andersenUnknownyearascanningelectron pages 4-6) | Aim initially for roughly **1–1.5 million recorded total counts per final standard**, then validate on the actual SEM–EDS system; increase toward 2.5 million when minor constituents require it and the specimen tolerates the dose. |
| Replicate workflow | Split the intended total acquisition into multiple nominally identical spectra; compare them with the dose-independent mean reduced **χ²** metric, for which values near **1** indicate differences consistent with Poisson statistics. Check each spectrum’s **Duane–Hunt limit**, reject anomalous spectra iteratively, and sum the consistent subset. (ritchie2022strategiesforstandardizing pages 1-3) | Replicates expose contamination, roughness, inhomogeneity, charging, beam-energy errors, and other failures that a single long spectrum can conceal. |
| Four 60-second acquisitions | **Four × 60 s** is a reasonable implementation of the replicate-and-sum strategy, but it is **not a NIST-mandated recipe**; earlier NIST work suggested approximately **5–10** subdivisions as another implementation. (ritchie2022strategiesforstandardizing pages 1-3, ritchie2018exploringthelimits pages 4-5) | Use four acquisitions only if they produce adequate counts and mutually consistent spectra. Verify current and live time, acceptable dead time/pileup, homogeneous raster placement, absence of drift or contamination, and no beam-induced damage before summing. |


*Table: A compact distinction between formal NIST guidance, empirical count targets, and the recommended replicate-screen-and-sum workflow for measured EDS standards.*

## Recommended acquisition practice

The recommended NIST strategy is indeed to acquire **multiple nominally identical point or small-raster spectra**, rather than one uninterrupted long spectrum. Divide total intended time \(\tau\) among \(M\) acquisitions of approximately \(\tau/M\), compare them, reject anomalous members, and sum only the self-consistent subset. DTSA-II’s Spectrum Bundler implements this concept. NIST uses a dose-independent mean reduced-\(\chi^2\) comparison: values near unity indicate differences consistent with Poisson counting statistics; high-scoring spectra are removed iteratively. Every candidate should also pass a Duane–Hunt-limit check for beam-energy/charging problems. (ritchie2022strategiesforstandardizing pages 1-3)

Earlier NIST work suggested approximately **5–10 subdivisions**, but the principle—not a fixed replicate number—is important. (ritchie2018exploringthelimits pages 4-5)

Therefore, **four 60-s point/raster acquisitions, outlier checking, and summing are reasonable practice**, but “4 × 60 s” is not a NIST-prescribed recipe. It is appropriate only if:

- the retained sum reaches adequate recorded counts—practically, often around **1–1.5 million or more**;
- all spectra were collected at the same beam energy, geometry, detector settings, and controlled probe current;
- dead time and pileup remain acceptable;
- the raster lies wholly within a flat, homogeneous region representing the intended standard;
- no charging, drift, contamination, oxidation, or beam-induced compositional change occurs;
- individual live times/doses are correctly preserved and combined; and
- replicate spectra agree statistically before summation.

For heterogeneous AlSi10Mg, a bulk alloy spectrum is generally not an ideal element-specific measured standard unless its composition and homogeneity at the interaction-volume/raster scale are established. Pure Al, pure Si, or certified homogeneous compounds/alloys are preferable measured references; NIST authors prefer pure elements where practical and stable stoichiometric compounds when elemental standards are unsuitable. (newbury2019electronexcitedxraymicroanalysis pages 3-4)

(pqac-00000018) | Specify and preserve current, live time, detector conditions, and resulting counts rather than treating “60 s” alone as a sufficient dose specification. |
| Empirical count guidance | Instrument-specific testing found that about **0.5 million total counts** could give **<2% RSD for major elements**; **1–1.5 million** was a practical baseline, with diminishing returns above this range. Counts up to **2.5 million** still improved some minor-element results. (pqac-00000019) | Aim initially for roughly **1–1.5 million recorded total counts per final standard**, then validate on the actual SEM–EDS system; increase toward 2.5 million when minor constituents require it and the specimen tolerates the dose. |
| Replicate workflow | Split the intended total acquisition into multiple nominally identical spectra; compare them with the dose-independent mean reduced **χ²** metric, for which values near **1** indicate differences consistent with Poisson statistics. Check each spectrum’s **Duane–Hunt limit**, reject anomalous spectra iteratively, and sum the consistent subset. (pqac-00000018) | Replicates expose contamination, roughness, inhomogeneity, charging, beam-energy errors, and other failures that a single long spectrum can conceal. |
| Four 60-second acquisitions | **Four × 60 s** is a reasonable implementation of the replicate-and-sum strategy, but it is **not a NIST-mandated recipe**; earlier NIST work suggested approximately **5–10** subdivisions as another implementation. (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000003) | Use four acquisitions only if they produce adequate counts and mutually consistent spectra. Verify current and live time, acceptable dead time/pileup, homogeneous raster placement, absence of drift or contamination, and no beam-induced damage before summing. |


*Table: A compact distinction between formal NIST guidance, empirical count targets, and the recommended replicate-screen-and-sum workflow for measured EDS standards.*

info.query: In NIST DTSA-II, creating a quantification standard from a measured EDS spectrum requires adequate counting statistics. Why would a spectrum extracted or summed from an EDS spectrum-image (X-ray map) of an AlSi10Mg alloy fail signal-to-noise or precision checks even for major elements like Al and Si? What total counts or dose are recommended for standard spectra, and is the recommended practice to acquire several long point/raster spectra (e.g. four 60-second acquisitions), check for outliers, and sum them?
